notes.meaning: This entry lists ninety-five people connected to the town of Gibeon. Earlier verses grouped returnees by family heads, but here the list begins naming people by their home towns. God took careful note of those who were willing to return and rebuild their ancestral homes.

A total of 188 men returned from Bethlehem and the nearby town of Netophah in Judah. Bethlehem was the famous home of King David and the promised birthplace of the Messiah. These neighboring communities are counted together here as they came home to reoccupy their land.

These verses count 128 men from Anathoth and 42 men from Beth-azmaveth, both located in the land of Benjamin. Anathoth was well known as a town for priests and the home of the prophet Jeremiah. Even very small villages had faithful families who returned after decades in exile.

The towns of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth sent back 743 men together. Kiriath-jearim had a long history in Israel as the town where the Ark of the Covenant rested before King David brought it to Jerusalem. Returning to these historic places reminded the people of God's past mercies.

Here 621 men from Ramah and Geba are listed, along with 122 men from Michmash. These places in Benjamin played important parts in early Bible history, including the days of Samuel and King Saul. God remembered these communities and preserved their families through long years in Babylon.

Bethel and Ai supplied 123 men, while fifty-two came from the other Nebo. Bethel was famous as the holy place where God met Jacob, and Ai was known from the time of Joshua. This Nebo is called 'the other' to keep it distinct from the town of Nebo located east of the Jordan River.

A second family named Elam numbered 1,254 men, and Harim's family numbered 320. This Elam is called 'the other' so readers would not confuse his household with the Elam mentioned earlier in the list. God kept each large family safe and restored them to their rightful inheritance.

This group closes the list of regular citizens, recording 345 from Jericho, 721 from Lod, Hadid, and Ono, and 3,930 from Senaah. Senaah formed the largest single clan among the returning townspeople. Counting every settlement proved that God was rebuilding the whole nation town by town.

The record moves to the priests, starting with 973 men from the family of Jedaiah through the house of Jeshua. Only four of the twenty-four official groups of priests set up by King David returned from the exile. Jedaiah was closely related to the high priest who helped lead the people back to Jerusalem.

These verses list the remaining three priestly lines: Immer with 1,052 men, Pashhur with 1,247, and Harim with 1,017. Priests had to prove their family line back to Aaron so they could serve lawfully at the altar. God preserved these families so worship at the temple could continue as the law required.

Only seventy-four Levites returned from Babylon, all belonging to the family of Jeshua through Kadmiel and Hodevah. Levites were tribe members set apart to help the priests and look after God's house. Although far fewer Levites returned than priests, God took special notice of the few who were willing to come.

The temple choir consisted of 148 singers from the family of Asaph. Asaph was the chief worship leader appointed by King David to write and sing praises to the Lord. His family returned to make sure music and thanksgiving were restored in the rebuilt temple.

Six families of gatekeepers returned, adding up to 138 men. These men were responsible for opening the temple gates, guarding the holy rooms, and protecting the sacred vessels. Because they were trained watchmen, Nehemiah also called on them to help guard the gates of the rebuilt city.

These verses begin the list of temple servants, naming the families of Ziha, Hasupha, Tabbaoth, Keros, Sia, and Padon. These workers were helpers originally appointed in David's time to carry wood, fetch water, and assist the Levites. Even though their duties were humble, the Lord valued their work and recorded their names.

The list of temple servants continues with the families of Lebanah, Hagabah, Shalmai, Hanan, Giddel, and Gahar. These families gave up their lives in Babylon to perform the quiet, everyday tasks needed to keep God's house open. God honors faithful and willing service, no matter how small it may seem.
